structure.title: Chapters 1–6 · Sara arrives at school
structure.text: Captain Crewe's money buys a sitting room, a doll with a wardrobe and Miss Minchin's devoted attention. Sara would like to believe she can tell the difference between affection and deference. Her early friendships put that confidence to a gentler test than the adults will.

structure.title: Chapters 7–9 · A birthday changes her place in the house
structure.text: News reaching the school during a party changes what Sara may eat, wear and call her own. She can cross the same landing as yesterday and be ordered about by someone who then wished to please her. Her stories now have to sustain a hungry storyteller as well as an audience.

structure.title: Chapters 10–19 · The rooms on either side of the wall
structure.text: A neighbouring house comes into view from the attic. Sara and the reader know different pieces of what is happening across the roof. Burnett can turn a blanket or a hot meal into a marvel because she has shown us exactly how much work it takes to do without one.

people.name: Sara and Becky
people.text: Becky hears Sara tell stories while doing her work. Long before Sara understands what hunger costs, Becky has to decide whether a few extra minutes of listening are worth the risk of being caught away from her duties.

people.name: Miss Minchin
people.text: Her school sells a respectable upbringing. A wealthy pupil can be shown off to prospective customers, while an unpaid bill feels like a personal affront. The speed of her changes in manner lets a child see the accounts underneath the compliments.

context.title: A princess as an experiment
context.text: Sara tries imagining that she is a princess when somebody provokes her. The game lets her choose how a powerful person ought to behave while she is standing among people with actual power. Its costs become clearer once politeness wins her neither food nor protection.

notice.text: Notice who gets a second helping.
notice.why: Food passes between people with sharply different appetites and resources. A bun generously given when one has several to spare means something quite different to the child going hungry herself.

notice.text: Compare an attic story with a practical kindness.
notice.why: Sara can turn a bare room into a palace for the duration of a tale. Someone still has to light a fire and provide the bedclothes before a child can sleep there in comfort. The novel gives room to both kinds of invention.

opening: Sara Crewe arrives at boarding school with expensive clothes, a devoted father, and a headmistress eager to please. When the money disappears, the same adults discover reasons to treat her quite differently. Sara is sent upstairs to work and sleep in the cold, carrying an imagination that had once looked like another luxury. Burnett makes kindness matter in small, material ways: a shared meal, a word of recognition, the decision to regard someone as a person when the household has decided she is useful labour.
